title: Glaucoma: angle anatomy, POAG vs PACG vs congenital, drugs & surgery
subject: Ophthalmology
anchor: Painless, slowly progressive peripheral field loss + vertical cup enlargement + raised IOP + open angle → POAG
Hypermetrope, dim light/evening, severe pain, haloes, vomiting, stony-hard red eye, vertically oval mid-dilated fixed pupil, shallow AC → acute PACG
Infant with photophobia, epiphora, blepharospasm, large hazy cornea (>12 mm), Haab striae → primary congenital glaucoma (buphthalmos)
algorithm:
Acute primary angle closure (IOP often 50–70 mmHg)
  → Lower IOP first: IV mannitol 20% (or oral glycerol) + IV/oral acetazolamide + topical timolol / α2 agonist + topical steroid
  → Pilocarpine 2% once IOP falls (ischaemic iris sphincter does not respond at very high IOP)
  → Definitive: Nd:YAG laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) in BOTH eyes (fellow eye prophylactic)
  → >50% of angle closed by peripheral anterior synechiae / uncontrolled → trabeculectomy
POAG
  → PG analogue first line → add β-blocker / CAI / α2 agonist
  → SLT (selective laser trabeculoplasty) as first-line or add-on
  → Uncontrolled / progressing → trabeculectomy with MMC or 5-FU → glaucoma drainage device
Primary congenital glaucoma → SURGERY is primary
  → Goniotomy (clear cornea) or trabeculotomy (hazy cornea) → combined trabeculotomy + trabeculectomy
  → Drugs only to clear cornea / temporise before surgery

points: Gonioscopy angle structures (posterior → anterior): iris root, ciliary body band, scleral spur, trabecular meshwork, Schwalbe line (end of Descemet); Shaffer grade 0 = closed, 4 = wide open.

**Earliest clinically significant field defect** in POAG: isolated paracentral scotoma in Bjerrum area (10–20° from fixation) → Seidel (sickle) scotoma → arcuate (Bjerrum) scotoma → Roenne nasal step → ring scotoma → tubular vision → temporal island (last to go).

Glaucomatous disc: vertical cup enlargement, C:D asymmetry >0.2 between eyes, inferior > superior rim thinning (ISNT rule violated), splinter (Drance) haemorrhage, bayoneting & nasal shift of vessels, laminar dot sign.
PACG risk: hypermetropia, short axial length, shallow AC, thick anteriorly placed lens, female, Asian; provocative tests: dark room, prone, mydriatic.
Haab striae = horizontal/curvilinear breaks in Descemet membrane (congenital glaucoma); forceps-injury breaks are vertical/oblique. CYP1B1 is the main gene in primary congenital glaucoma.
Trabeculectomy = guarded partial-thickness scleral flap fistula draining into a subconjunctival filtering bleb; antimetabolites (MMC/5-FU) reduce bleb fibrosis.
Neovascular glaucoma (ischaemic CRVO, PDR) – '100-day glaucoma' after CRVO; treat with anti-VEGF + PRP ± drainage device.

Lens-induced: phacomorphic (swollen intumescent lens → secondary angle closure) vs phacolytic (hypermature lens proteins leak through intact capsule → macrophages block open angle) → both need cataract extraction.
Steroid-induced glaucoma (open angle) – topical steroids most often; pseudoexfoliation and pigment dispersion (Krukenberg spindle) are other secondary open-angle causes.

traps.stem: Multiple-correct: which are components of the trabecular meshwork?
traps.trap: Ticking Schlemm's canal or scleral spur because they sit in the same angle region.
traps.fix: Only uveal (inner), corneoscleral (middle) and juxtacanalicular (outer) meshwork; the juxtacanalicular layer gives the main resistance. Schlemm's canal is the collecting channel, not a layer.

traps.stem: Acute angle closure, IOP 62 mmHg, pupil fixed and mid-dilated. Best first drug?
traps.trap: Pilocarpine alone first – it is the 'miotic for angle closure'.
traps.fix: At very high IOP the iris sphincter is ischaemic and unresponsive; first lower IOP with IV mannitol + acetazolamide + timolol, then pilocarpine; definitive = LPI in both eyes.

traps.stem: A 60-year-old asthmatic with POAG needs medical therapy.
traps.trap: Timolol – cheapest, classic first drug.
traps.fix: Non-selective β-blockers are contraindicated in asthma; use a PG analogue (latanoprost) as first line.

cards.text: The main site of resistance to aqueous outflow is the {{c1::juxtacanalicular (cribriform) meshwork}}, the {{c2::outermost}} trabecular layer lining Schlemm's canal.

cards.front: Anti-glaucoma drug that darkens the iris and lengthens eyelashes – mechanism?
cards.back: Prostaglandin analogue (latanoprost) – ↑ uveoscleral outflow.

cards.front: Earliest clinically significant field defect in POAG?
cards.back: Isolated paracentral scotoma in Bjerrum's area (10–20°); temporal island is the last to be lost.

cards.text: Definitive treatment of acute primary angle closure is {{c1::Nd:YAG laser peripheral iridotomy}}, performed in {{c2::both eyes (fellow eye prophylactically)}}.

cards.front: Haab striae: orientation and meaning?
cards.back: Horizontal/curvilinear Descemet breaks from corneal stretching in congenital glaucoma (birth-trauma breaks are vertical/oblique).

cards.front: Glaucoma drug contraindicated in infants <2 years?
cards.back: Brimonidine (α2 agonist) – crosses blood–brain barrier → CNS depression, apnoea.

cards.front: Discriminator: POAG vs primary angle closure — deciding feature?
cards.back: POAG: open angle on gonioscopy, painless, cupping. PACG: shallow chamber, narrow angle, painful red eye, halos, mid-dilated fixed pupil, steamy cornea.

images.caption: Advanced glaucomatous cupping: large vertical cup with thin neuroretinal rim and nasal displacement/bayoneting of vessels.
Buphthalmos from congenital glaucoma: enlarged globe and cornea (>12 mm in infancy) – surgery (goniotomy/trabeculotomy) is primary treatment.

title: Pupil & neuro-ophthalmology: RAPD, abnormal pupils, disc swelling, orbital apex
subject: Ophthalmology
anchor: Swinging flashlight: affected pupil dilates when light swings onto it → RAPD (Marcus Gunn pupil) = optic nerve or extensive retinal disease
Painful ophthalmoplegia (III, IV, VI, V1) + RAPD/↓ vision → orbital apex; same without vision loss → superior orbital fissure; + V2 / Horner / bilateral → cavernous sinus
Young woman, ↓ vision over days, pain on eye movement, red desaturation, RAPD, normal disc → retrobulbar optic neuritis
Ptosis + miosis + anhidrosis; apraclonidine reverses anisocoria → Horner syndrome
algorithm:
Third nerve palsy
  → Pupil involved (dilated, non-reactive) = 'surgical' → urgent CTA/MRA for posterior communicating artery aneurysm (pupillomotor fibres are superficial, dorsomedial)
  → Pupil spared, complete motor palsy, diabetic/hypertensive = 'medical' (microvascular infarct of nerve core) → observe; recovers in ~3 months
  → Partial palsy or young patient → image anyway
Suspected Horner
  → Cocaine 4–10%: Horner pupil fails to dilate (confirms) | Apraclonidine 0.5–1%: Horner pupil dilates + lid rises (reversal of anisocoria; denervation supersensitivity)
  → Hydroxyamphetamine 1% (localises, ≥24–48 h later): dilates = 1st/2nd-order (preganglionic); fails = 3rd-order (postganglionic)
Suspected giant cell arteritis (age >50, jaw claudication, ESR/CRP ↑)
  → Start high-dose steroids IMMEDIATELY → temporal artery biopsy within 1–2 weeks (does not wait for result)

points: **Superior orbital fissure syndrome**: III, IV, VI, V1 (+ superior ophthalmic vein) → ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, forehead numbness; vision normal.
**Orbital apex syndrome** = SOF syndrome + optic nerve (II) → ↓ vision, RAPD.

**Cavernous sinus**: III, IV, V1, V2, VI + sympathetic plexus (Horner possible), may become bilateral; CN VI (free in the sinus) often affected first; chemosis/proptosis in thrombosis or carotid-cavernous fistula (bruit, corkscrew vessels).

**Tolosa–Hunt syndrome**: idiopathic granulomatous inflammation of cavernous sinus/SOF → painful ophthalmoplegia with dramatic response to steroids; diagnosis of exclusion (MRI, rule out tumour/infection).

RAPD causes: optic neuritis, ischaemic optic neuropathy, compressive optic neuropathy, asymmetric advanced glaucoma, CRAO, large retinal detachment; optic tract lesion → contralateral RAPD. NOT caused by cataract, refractive error or corneal opacity.
Light–near dissociation: Argyll Robertson, Adie, Parinaud dorsal midbrain syndrome, diabetes, aberrant III regeneration.
Retrobulbar neuritis: 'patient sees nothing, doctor sees nothing'; Uhthoff phenomenon (worse with heat/exercise); test MOG and AQP4 antibodies in atypical/severe cases (NMOSD).
Foster Kennedy syndrome: ipsilateral optic atrophy + contralateral papilloedema – olfactory groove/sphenoid wing meningioma; pseudo-Foster Kennedy = sequential NA-AION.

Horner: 1st-order (hypothalamus→C8–T2: Wallenberg, syrinx), 2nd-order (preganglionic: Pancoast, neck surgery), 3rd-order (postganglionic: carotid dissection, cluster headache, cavernous sinus); anhidrosis absent/limited in 3rd-order lesions beyond the carotid bifurcation.

traps.stem: Painful ophthalmoplegia (III, IV, VI), forehead numbness AND a RAPD with ↓ vision. Site?
traps.trap: Superior orbital fissure or cavernous sinus – both give painful III/IV/VI/V1 palsy.
traps.fix: RAPD/↓ vision means the optic nerve is involved → orbital apex syndrome (optic canal + SOF).

traps.stem: Pain on eye movement, marked RAPD, normal-looking disc – but full ocular motility.
traps.trap: Calling it orbital apex/Tolosa–Hunt because of pain and RAPD.
traps.fix: Preserved motility = no true ophthalmoplegia → retrobulbar optic neuritis.

traps.stem: Diabetic with painful third nerve palsy and a dilated, unreactive pupil.
traps.trap: Diabetic microvascular palsy – observe.
traps.fix: Pupil involvement = compressive (PComm aneurysm) until proven otherwise → urgent CTA/MRA.

cards.front: Pharmacological test that confirms Horner by REVERSAL of anisocoria?
cards.back: Apraclonidine 0.5–1%: the Horner pupil dilates (α1 denervation supersensitivity) and the lid elevates; normal pupil unchanged/slightly smaller.

cards.text: Hydroxyamphetamine dilates the Horner pupil if the lesion is {{c1::pre-ganglionic (1st/2nd order)}} and fails if it is {{c2::post-ganglionic (3rd order)}}.

cards.front: Adie tonic pupil – diagnostic drop?
cards.back: Dilute pilocarpine 0.125%: constricts the Adie pupil (cholinergic denervation supersensitivity), not the normal pupil.

cards.text: Orbital apex syndrome = superior orbital fissure syndrome + involvement of {{c1::optic nerve (CN II)}}, producing {{c2::RAPD and visual loss}}.

cards.front: Field defect typical of anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy?
cards.back: Altitudinal defect (usually inferior).

cards.front: Third nerve palsy: why is the pupil spared in diabetes but involved with aneurysm?
cards.back: Pupillomotor fibres lie superficially (dorsomedial) – compressed by aneurysm; diabetic ischaemia affects the core of the nerve.

title: Optics & instruments sheet: Volk lenses, ophthalmoscopes, Hofstetter, retinoscopy, dark adaptation
subject: Ophthalmology
anchor: Slit-lamp (Volk) lens: HIGHER dioptre → LOWER magnification: 60D ≈1.15× > 78D ≈0.93× > 90D ≈0.76×
Direct ophthalmoscope ≈15×, virtual erect image, small field | Indirect ≈3× with +20D (60/20), real inverted image, wide stereoscopic field
Hofstetter (amplitude of accommodation, D; A = age in years): Minimum 15 − 0.25A | Mean 18.5 − 0.3A | Maximum 25 − 0.4A
algorithm:
Hofstetter worked example – 7-year-old child
  → Minimum = 15 − 0.25 × 7 = 15 − 1.75 = 13.25 D
  → Mean (average) = 18.5 − 0.3 × 7 = 18.5 − 2.1 = 16.4 D
  → Maximum = 25 − 0.4 × 7 = 25 − 2.8 = 22.2 D
  → Near point (emmetrope) ≈ 100 / amplitude cm → 100/16.4 ≈ 6 cm
Retinoscopy (plane mirror, working distance 1 m → subtract 1 D; at 66 cm subtract 1.5 D)
  → 'With' movement: hypermetropia, emmetropia, or myopia < 1 D
  → 'Against' movement: myopia > 1 D
  → No movement (neutral): far point at the observer's eye (myopia of 1 D at 1 m)
  → Final refraction = neutralising lens − working-distance correction

points: Rule: lens power ∝ field of view (generally), inversely ∝ magnification – 90D trades magnification for field; 60D gives the largest image.

**Dark adaptation sequence**: pupil dilates (immediate) → cone threshold falls and plateaus (~5–10 min) → rod–cone break (~7–10 min) → rod sensitivity rises as rhodopsin regenerates (11-cis retinal + opsin; needs vitamin A) → complete at ~30–40 min. Light adaptation is much faster.
Delayed dark adaptation / night blindness: vitamin A deficiency, retinitis pigmentosa, congenital stationary night blindness, Oguchi disease (Mizuo phenomenon), gyrate atrophy.
Refractive power: total ≈ +58–60 D; cornea ≈ +43 D (≈2/3, the major refracting surface); crystalline lens ≈ +15–20 D (varies with accommodation).
Correction: myopia → concave (minus) lens; hypermetropia → convex (plus); astigmatism → cylinder; presbyopia → near add (near point recedes beyond ~25 cm, usually after 40 yr).
Aphakia: spectacle ≈ +10 to +11 D, ~25–30% image magnification, ring scotoma, 'jack-in-the-box' phenomenon; unilateral aphakic spectacles → aniseikonia/diplopia → contact lens or IOL.
Duochrome test: letters clearer on red → eye is relatively myopic (needs more minus); clearer on green → over-minused/hypermetropic.
Jackson cross-cylinder refines axis and power of astigmatic correction; with-the-rule astigmatism = vertical meridian steeper (common in young).
Anisometropia: difference >2.5–3 D is poorly tolerated with spectacles (aniseikonia) → contact lenses; leading cause of unilateral amblyopia.

traps.stem: Match: which Volk lens gives the HIGHEST magnification?
traps.trap: 90D – the 'strongest' lens sounds most magnifying.
traps.fix: 60D (≈1.15×); magnification falls as dioptric power rises (78D ≈0.93×, 90D ≈0.76×).

traps.stem: Average amplitude of accommodation of a 7-year-old by Hofstetter?
traps.trap: 13.25 D – applying the minimum formula (15 − 0.25A) because it is the one most often memorised.
traps.fix: Average = 18.5 − 0.3A = 16.4 D; minimum 13.25 D; maximum 22.2 D – read which formula the stem asks.

traps.stem: Retinoscopy at 1 m with a plane mirror shows 'with' movement.
traps.trap: Hypermetropia only.
traps.fix: With movement at 1 m = hypermetropia, emmetropia, or myopia <1 D; always subtract the working-distance dioptres.

cards.text: Hofstetter: minimum = {{c1::15 − 0.25 × age}}, mean = {{c2::18.5 − 0.3 × age}}, maximum = {{c3::25 − 0.4 × age}} dioptres.

cards.front: Direct vs indirect ophthalmoscope – magnification and image?
cards.back: Direct ≈15×, virtual erect, small field. Indirect ≈3× with +20D lens (60/20), real inverted, wide stereoscopic field.

cards.front: What is the rod–cone break (Kohlrausch kink)?
cards.back: The point (~7–10 min into dark adaptation) where rod sensitivity overtakes the plateaued cone threshold.

cards.front: Gonioscopy mirror of the Goldmann 3-mirror lens?
cards.back: The smallest, dome-shaped 59° mirror – views the angle and extreme periphery/ora.

title: Retina: diabetic & hypertensive retinopathy, CRAO/CRVO, ROP, RD, retinoblastoma
subject: Ophthalmology
anchor: Diabetic: microaneurysms (earliest clinical sign) → dot-blot haemorrhages, hard exudates; NVD/NVE = proliferative DR; vision loss mostly from macular oedema
Sudden painless profound loss, milky white retina, cherry-red spot, box-carring of arterioles → CRAO | 'blood and thunder' fundus, tortuous veins → CRVO
Preterm <34 wk or <2000 g (India) → ROP screening; leukocoria in a child under 5 → retinoblastoma until proven otherwise
algorithm:
Diabetic eye disease
  → Screening: type 1 – 5 yr after diagnosis (from puberty); type 2 – at diagnosis; pregnancy – early first trimester
  → Centre-involving DME with vision loss → intravitreal anti-VEGF first line (ranibizumab / aflibercept / bevacizumab); dexamethasone implant 2nd line
  → Non-centre CSME → focal/grid laser (ETDRS)
  → High-risk PDR → panretinal photocoagulation (anti-VEGF an alternative)
  → Non-clearing vitreous haemorrhage / tractional RD threatening macula → pars plana vitrectomy
ROP (India: screen <34 wk GA or <2000 g; also 34–36 wk / 2000–2500 g with risk factors)
  → First exam by day 20–30 of life (earlier in <28 wk / <1200 g)
  → Type 1 ROP (treat within 48–72 h): zone I any stage with plus; zone I stage 3 without plus; zone II stage 2 or 3 with plus
  → Laser ablation of avascular retina; anti-VEGF (esp. zone I / aggressive ROP)
  → Type 2 ROP → close follow-up

points: Earliest histological change in DR: thickening of capillary basement membrane and **pericyte loss**; earliest clinical sign: microaneurysms; most common cause of vision loss: diabetic macular oedema.

Hypertensive retinopathy (Keith–Wagener–Barker): I – mild arteriolar narrowing; II – AV nipping (Salus/Gunn sign), focal narrowing; III – + flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, hard exudates (macular star); IV – + papilloedema.

**CRAO**: emboli (carotid cholesterol = Hollenhorst plaque), GCA (check ESR/CRP); cherry-red spot = intact choroid visible through thin foveola lacking ganglion cells, against opaque ischaemic retina; cilioretinal artery (present in a minority) spares central vision; irreversible damage within ~90–100 min.
Cherry-red spot differential: CRAO, Tay–Sachs, Sandhoff, Niemann–Pick, GM1 gangliosidosis, Farber, sialidosis, commotio retinae (Berlin oedema).

**CRVO**: age, HTN, diabetes, glaucoma (raised IOP), hyperviscosity; ischaemic type (>10 disc areas of non-perfusion on FFA, RAPD) → iris neovascularisation → neovascular glaucoma ('100-day glaucoma'); macular oedema → anti-VEGF. BRVO most often superotemporal (at AV crossings).

**ROP**: zone I = circle centred on disc with radius twice disc–fovea distance; zone II to nasal ora; zone III residual temporal crescent. Stages: 1 demarcation line, 2 ridge, 3 extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation, 4 partial RD (4A extrafoveal, 4B foveal), 5 total RD. Plus disease = dilated tortuous posterior pole vessels.

**Retinoblastoma**: RB1 on 13q14 (Knudson two-hit); most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood; leukocoria (most common sign) > strabismus; calcification on USG/CT; Flexner–Wintersteiner rosettes (Homer Wright also), fleurettes (retinocytoma); bilateral = germline → screen siblings, risk of pinealoblastoma (trilateral RB) and osteosarcoma.

Retinoblastoma spread mainly along optic nerve → enucleate with long optic nerve stump (≥10 mm); treatment: chemoreduction (vincristine–etoposide–carboplatin) + focal therapy, intra-arterial chemo, enucleation for advanced.
Leukocoria differentials: retinoblastoma, congenital cataract, Coats disease, persistent fetal vasculature (PHPV), ROP stage 5, toxocariasis, coloboma.

traps.stem: Fundus: haemorrhages in all four quadrants, no new vessels. Grade?
traps.trap: PDR because the fundus looks very 'busy'.
traps.fix: Severe NPDR (one 4-2-1 criterion). PDR requires neovascularisation (NVD/NVE) or pre-retinal/vitreous haemorrhage.

traps.stem: Why is the macula red in CRAO?
traps.trap: Haemorrhage at the fovea.
traps.fix: The foveola has no ganglion cell/inner layers, so the normal choroidal circulation shows through while the surrounding ischaemic inner retina turns opaque white.

traps.stem: Child with leukocoria and suspected bilateral retinoblastoma – imaging of choice?
traps.trap: CT orbit (shows calcification best – the classic textbook line).
traps.fix: Exam-classic: CT demonstrates calcification. | Current practice: USG (B-scan) + MRI orbit/brain; avoid CT radiation in germline RB1 (risk of second cancers).

cards.text: Severe NPDR (4-2-1 rule): haemorrhages in {{c1::4}} quadrants, venous beading in {{c2::2}} quadrants, IRMA in {{c3::1}} quadrant.

cards.front: First-line treatment of centre-involving diabetic macular oedema with vision loss?
cards.back: Intravitreal anti-VEGF (ranibizumab, aflibercept, bevacizumab). Focal laser was the classic ETDRS answer.

cards.text: ROP screening in India: all babies born at {{c1::< 34 weeks}} gestation or birth weight {{c2::< 2000 g}}.

cards.front: Type 1 ROP (treat) criteria?
cards.back: Zone I any stage with plus; zone I stage 3 without plus; zone II stage 2 or 3 with plus.

cards.front: Retinal detachment with shifting subretinal fluid and no break?
cards.back: Exudative RD (e.g. VKH, posterior scleritis, choroidal tumour, pre-eclampsia) – treat the cause.

cards.text: Retinoblastoma gene {{c1::RB1}} lies on chromosome {{c2::13q14}}; most common presenting sign is {{c3::leukocoria}}.

cards.front: Discriminator: Papilloedema vs optic neuritis — deciding feature?
cards.back: Papilloedema: bilateral, vision normal early, enlarged blind spot, raised ICP. Optic neuritis: unilateral, ↓vision, painful eye movement, RAPD, colour desaturation (MS).

images.caption: Proliferative diabetic retinopathy: new vessels/fibrovascular tissue on the retinal surface – NVD/NVE define PDR.
CRAO: pale oedematous retina with cherry-red spot at the fovea and attenuated arterioles.
Leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) in retinoblastoma – commonest presenting sign.

title: EOMs & squint, blow-out fracture, thyroid eye, chemical injury, NPCBVI, trachoma
subject: Ophthalmology
anchor: Diplopia on upgaze + enophthalmos + cheek numbness after a punch → orbital floor blow-out fracture (inferior rectus entrapment)
Lid retraction + lid lag + proptosis, restricted elevation, fusiform muscle bellies with tendon sparing → thyroid eye disease
Chemical splash → IRRIGATE first, before history or visual acuity
TF/TI/TS/TT/CO and SAFE → trachoma (Chlamydia trachomatis A–C)

Paralytic (incomitant)
Concomitant

points: Clinical testing positions: SR – abduction + elevation; IR – abduction + depression; IO – adduction + elevation; SO – adduction + depression.
Hirschberg corneal reflex: at pupil margin ≈15°, midway pupil–limbus ≈30°, at limbus ≈45° of deviation. Cover test detects manifest squint; cover–uncover/alternate cover detects latent (phoria).
Amblyopia: patch (occlude) the good eye or atropine penalisation; best results before ~7–8 years.

**Blow-out fracture**: floor (posteromedial maxillary roof, over infraorbital canal) ± medial wall (lamina papyracea); enophthalmos, diplopia on upgaze, infraorbital anaesthesia, emphysema on nose-blowing; teardrop sign; CT (coronal) investigation of choice. Child with 'white-eyed' trapdoor fracture + bradycardia/vomiting (oculocardiac reflex) → urgent release.

**Thyroid eye disease**: most common cause of unilateral and bilateral proptosis in adults; lid retraction is the commonest sign (Dalrymple), von Graefe = lid lag on downgaze; muscles: IR > MR > SR > LR; tendon-sparing fusiform enlargement; compressive optic neuropathy → IV methylprednisolone / orbital decompression; smoking and radioiodine worsen; teprotumumab (IGF-1R antibody).

**Chemical injury**: alkali worse than acid (saponification, deep penetration; acid coagulates surface proteins – except hydrofluoric acid); irrigate copiously (≥30 min / until pH neutral), double-evert lids; limbal ischaemia grades severity (Roper-Hall/Dua); late: symblepharon, limbal stem cell deficiency.

**NPCB** launched 1976 (100% centrally sponsored) → renamed NPCBVI (2017). Vision 2020: Right to Sight launched 1999 by WHO + IAPB. India blindness definition (2017, WHO-aligned): presenting VA <3/60 in better eye (earlier <6/60) or field <10°. Cataract = leading cause of blindness in India.

**Trachoma (WHO simplified grading)**: TF ≥5 follicles (≥0.5 mm) on upper tarsus; TI inflammatory thickening obscuring >half of deep tarsal vessels; TS tarsal scarring; TT ≥1 lash touching globe; CO corneal opacity over pupil. Herbert pits (pathognomonic), Arlt line, superior pannus.

**SAFE**: Surgery for TT, Antibiotics (single-dose azithromycin 20 mg/kg, max 1 g; mass treatment when TF ≥10% in 1–9-year-olds), Facial cleanliness, Environmental improvement. Elimination targets: TF <5% in 1–9 yr and TT <0.2% in ≥15 yr; WHO validated India as having eliminated trachoma as a public health problem (2024).

title: Audiology: tuning forks, PTA, tympanometry, BERA/OAE, otosclerosis, Ménière, acoustic neuroma
subject: ENT
anchor: Young woman, bilateral progressive conductive deafness, normal TM, hears better in noise (paracusis Willisii), worse in pregnancy → otosclerosis; As tympanogram, absent stapedial reflex, Carhart notch at 2 kHz
Episodic vertigo (20 min–12 h) + fluctuating low-frequency SNHL + tinnitus + aural fullness → Ménière's disease
Unilateral progressive SNHL with speech discrimination worse than pure-tone loss, ↓ corneal reflex → vestibular schwannoma → gadolinium MRI
algorithm:
Newborn hearing screening (1-3-6: screen by 1 month, diagnose by 3, intervene by 6)
  → Well baby: OAE (otoacoustic emissions) → refer → automated ABR → diagnostic BERA
  → NICU baby / risk factors: automated ABR directly (OAE misses auditory neuropathy)
Tuning fork (512 Hz)
  → Rinne negative (BC > AC) + Weber to SAME ear → conductive loss in that ear
  → Rinne positive + Weber to OPPOSITE ear → SNHL in the tested ear
  → Rinne negative + Weber to OPPOSITE ear → severe/dead ear: FALSE-NEGATIVE Rinne (cross-hearing by the other cochlea) → confirm with masking (Bárány noise box)

head: Type
Shape
Conditions

points: **Carhart notch**: dip in BONE conduction maximal at 2000 Hz in otosclerosis (mechanical artefact – disappears after stapedotomy). **4 kHz notch (boilermaker's)**: noise-induced hearing loss. Presbycusis: bilateral high-frequency sloping SNHL.
Rinne with 512 Hz becomes negative only when the air–bone gap is ≥15–20 dB or more, so a 'positive' Rinne does not exclude a mild conductive loss.

Stapedial reflex arc: CN VIII afferent → superior olivary complex → CN VII efferent (stapedius). Absent in otosclerosis; reflex decay suggests retrocochlear lesion; recruitment (cochlear lesions) e.g. Ménière.

BERA waves (E-COLI): I – distal VIII nerve, II – proximal VIII/cochlear nucleus, III – superior olivary complex, IV – lateral lemniscus, V – inferior colliculus. Acoustic neuroma → prolonged I–V interpeak latency / delayed wave V.
OAE arise from OUTER hair cells; absent when hearing loss >~30–40 dB; present in auditory neuropathy (where ABR is abnormal).

**Otosclerosis**: autosomal dominant with variable penetrance, female, bilateral, worse in pregnancy; fissula ante fenestram (anterior to oval window) is the commonest site; **Schwartze sign** = flamingo-pink blush on promontory (active otospongiosis); treatment stapedotomy/stapedectomy with prosthesis, hearing aid; sodium fluoride for active/cochlear disease.

**Ménière's**: endolymphatic hydrops; glycerol test, ECochG (raised SP/AP ratio); treatment – salt restriction, betahistine, vestibular sedatives in acute attack, intratympanic gentamicin/steroid, endolymphatic sac surgery, vestibular neurectomy (hearing-preserving), labyrinthectomy (dead ear). Tumarkin otolithic crisis = sudden drop attacks.

**Vestibular schwannoma**: most common cerebellopontine angle tumour; Hitselberger sign (↓ sensation posterior meatal wall, CN VII sensory); earliest cranial nerve sign beyond VIII is ↓ corneal reflex (V); bilateral = NF2; gadolinium-enhanced MRI is the investigation of choice.
Maximum conductive loss with intact TM and ossicular discontinuity ≈ 60 dB.

traps.fix: Weber away from the Rinne-negative ear = right dead/severe SNHL; the 'negative' Rinne is false (sound crossed to left cochlea). Confirm with masking.

traps.fix: BC dip at 2 kHz = Carhart notch (otosclerosis); 4 kHz dip = noise-induced hearing loss.

traps.trap: Type B always means fluid.
traps.fix: Check canal volume: normal volume → OME; large volume → perforation/patent grommet; small volume → wax/probe against canal wall.

cards.back: Lateralised to the right (diseased) ear.

cards.back: Inferior colliculus (lateral lemniscus termination) – most robust wave, used for threshold estimation.

subject: ENT
anchor: Scanty, foul-smelling discharge + attic/posterosuperior marginal perforation + white flakes → squamosal (unsafe) CSOM with cholesteatoma → mastoidectomy
Ear discharge + retro-orbital pain + diplopia (lateral rectus palsy) → Gradenigo syndrome (petrous apicitis)
Picket-fence fever + oedema over mastoid emissary vein (Griesinger sign) → lateral (sigmoid) sinus thrombosis

head: Segment
Feature / branch

Above oval window; commonest site of bony dehiscence

Exits stylomastoid foramen → pes anserinus in parotid: temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical

points: **Cholesteatoma** = keratinising stratified squamous epithelium in middle ear/mastoid with keratin debris ('skin in the wrong place'); erodes bone via osteoclasts/collagenase; primary acquired (retraction pocket theory) is commonest; commonest site attic/Prussak's space; congenital = white mass behind intact TM (anterosuperior).
Most commonly eroded ossicle: long process of incus; commonest labyrinthine fistula: lateral semicircular canal → positive fistula test.

Imaging: HRCT temporal bone shows bone erosion (scutum, ossicles, tegmen); **non-EPI DWI MRI** shows cholesteatoma as restricted diffusion – used for residual/recurrent disease (avoids second-look surgery).

Intratemporal complications: mastoiditis (Bezold abscess – under sternocleidomastoid; Citelli – digastric triangle; Luc – under temporalis/meatus without mastoid tenderness), petrositis (Gradenigo: otorrhoea + retro-orbital pain V + VI palsy), labyrinthitis, facial palsy.

Intracranial: meningitis (commonest), extradural abscess, subdural, brain abscess (temporal lobe > cerebellum; otogenic is a leading cause), lateral sinus thrombosis (Griesinger sign, Tobey–Ayer test, empty-delta sign on contrast CT/MR venography), otitic hydrocephalus.

**Bell's palsy**: idiopathic LMN palsy (HSV-1 implicated), onset <72 h, forehead involved; oral prednisolone within 72 h (e.g. 1 mg/kg/day, usually 60 mg/day × 5 days then taper, or 50 mg × 10 days); antivirals add little alone; eye protection; ~70–85% recover fully.
Prognostic test: ENoG between day 3 and 14 – >90% degeneration → consider decompression (Fisch). Sequelae: synkinesis, crocodile tears (gustatory lacrimation from aberrant regeneration).
**Ramsay Hunt** (VZV geniculate ganglion): vesicles in concha/EAC, severe pain, ± SNHL/vertigo; worse prognosis; acyclovir/valacyclovir + steroids.

Temporal bone fracture: longitudinal (commoner, ~80%) → conductive loss, CSF otorrhoea, facial palsy less common (~20%); transverse → SNHL/vertigo, facial palsy ~50%. Immediate complete post-traumatic palsy → explore/decompress; delayed onset → conservative.

  → Sit up, lean forward, pinch soft part of nose 10–20 min (Trotter's method) + ABC/resuscitate

points: **Little's area / Kiesselbach plexus** (anteroinferior septum): anterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine (septal branch), greater palatine, superior labial (septal branch of facial) arteries – 'LEGS'. Woodruff plexus (posterior lateral wall, below posterior end of inferior turbinate) – posterior bleeds in elderly hypertensives.

**Laryngeal carcinoma**: SCC; glottic most common overall and best prognosis (early hoarseness, true cords have sparse lymphatics → late node spread); supraglottic – rich lymphatics, early bilateral level II–III nodes, dysphagia; subglottic – rarest, stridor, prelaryngeal (Delphian), pretracheal/paratracheal nodes. Early glottic → RT or transoral laser; advanced → chemoradiation (organ preservation) or total laryngectomy.

**Laryngomalacia**: commonest cause of congenital stridor; omega-shaped epiglottis, short aryepiglottic folds; inspiratory stridor worse supine/crying/feeding, better prone; self-limiting by ~18–24 months; severe (failure to thrive, apnoea) → supraglottoplasty. Second commonest: vocal cord palsy.
Stridor level: inspiratory → supraglottic/glottic (extrathoracic); biphasic → glottic/subglottic; expiratory → intrathoracic trachea/bronchi.

Tracheostomy: through 2nd–4th tracheal rings (avoid 1st ring/cricoid → subglottic stenosis); Bjork (inferiorly based) flap in adults; vertical slit, no cartilage excision in children; emergency surgical airway = cricothyroidotomy through cricothyroid membrane, converted to tracheostomy within ~24–72 h. Late massive bleed → tracheo-innominate fistula.

**JNA**: almost exclusively adolescent males (testosterone-dependent), arises posterolateral nasal wall at sphenopalatine foramen, supplied by internal maxillary artery; Holman–Miller (antral) sign on CT/lateral X-ray; CECT/MRI ± angiography – biopsy contraindicated; pre-operative embolisation then endoscopic excision.

**Nasopharyngeal carcinoma**: EBV (IgA anti-VCA/EA), salted fish nitrosamines, Southern Chinese & NE India; bimodal with a peak in adolescence; arises in fossa of Rosenmüller; commonest presentation = neck node (upper jugular/posterior triangle); unilateral SOM in an adult; CN VI commonest cranial nerve palsy; Trotter triad (conductive deafness, immobile ipsilateral soft palate, neuralgic pain in V3 distribution); WHO type III undifferentiated commonest and radiosensitive → RT ± concurrent cisplatin (surgery not primary).
Unilateral foul blood-stained nasal discharge in a child → foreign body; in adult → malignancy until proven otherwise.

Adrenocortical suppression (11β-hydroxylase inhibition), myoclonus, highest PONV, pain on injection

points: **MAC** = alveolar concentration preventing movement in 50% of patients to surgical incision; inversely proportional to potency (Meyer–Overton: potency ∝ lipid solubility). Methoxyflurane – most potent (MAC 0.16), nephrotoxic (fluoride).

MAC ↓: increasing age (~6% per decade), pregnancy, hypothermia, opioids, benzodiazepines, α2 agonists, acute alcohol intoxication, hyponatraemia. MAC ↑: infants (peak ~6 months), hyperthermia, chronic alcoholism, hypernatraemia, red hair. Unchanged: sex, duration of anaesthesia, thyroid status, K⁺.
Blood:gas coefficient = speed (solubility in blood); oil:gas = potency.
All volatile agents + succinylcholine trigger malignant hyperthermia; N₂O, propofol, ketamine, opioids, NDMRs are safe.

**Opioids**: morphine – histamine release, active metabolite M6G accumulates in renal failure; fentanyl ~100× morphine, chest-wall rigidity with rapid bolus; sufentanil most potent clinically used; remifentanil – ester hydrolysed by non-specific plasma/tissue esterases, context-sensitive half-time ~3–4 min regardless of infusion length; pethidine – normeperidine seizures, serotonin syndrome with MAOIs, used for post-op shivering.
Naloxone reverses opioids but is shorter-acting than most → watch for re-narcotisation; buprenorphine is a partial agonist with high receptor affinity (hard to reverse).
Dexmedetomidine (α2 agonist): sedation and analgesia without respiratory depression ('cooperative sedation').
Intra-arterial thiopentone: leave cannula in situ, inject heparin, papaverine/lignocaine/prostacyclin, sympathetic (stellate/brachial plexus) block.

traps.stem: Patient with acute intermittent porphyria needs GA – induction agent?
traps.trap: Thiopentone – the 'classic' barbiturate induction agent.
traps.fix: Barbiturates induce ALA synthase and precipitate crises – absolutely contraindicated; propofol is safe.

traps.stem: Fastest induction and recovery among listed volatiles?
traps.trap: The agent with the highest MAC (most 'gas' needed) or halothane (high potency).
traps.fix: Speed depends on LOW blood:gas coefficient → desflurane (0.42) among volatiles; xenon overall; N₂O 0.47.

traps.stem: Child for gas induction – sevoflurane or desflurane?
traps.trap: Desflurane because it is faster.
traps.fix: Desflurane is pungent → coughing, breath-holding, laryngospasm; sevoflurane is the agent of choice for inhalational induction.

cards.front: Induction agent that causes adrenal suppression?
cards.back: Etomidate – inhibits 11β-hydroxylase.

cards.text: N₂O is avoided in {{c1::pneumothorax / bowel obstruction / middle-ear surgery}} because it {{c2::diffuses into and expands closed air spaces}}.

cards.front: Diffusion hypoxia – cause and prevention?
cards.back: At end of N₂O anaesthesia, outpouring of N₂O into alveoli dilutes O₂; give 100% O₂ for 5–10 minutes.

cards.text: MAC of sevoflurane ≈ {{c1::2%}}; desflurane ≈ {{c2::6%}}; isoflurane ≈ {{c3::1.15%}}.

cards.front: Induction agent of choice in hypovolaemic shock with bronchospasm?
cards.back: Ketamine – sympathomimetic and bronchodilator.

title: Neuromuscular blockers, malignant hyperthermia, airway assessment, local anaesthetics, neuraxial block, fasting
subject: Anesthesia
anchor: Fasciculations, no fade on TOF, worsened by neostigmine → depolarising block (succinylcholine)
Unexplained rise in EtCO₂ + tachycardia + masseter rigidity after sux/volatile → malignant hyperthermia → dantrolene
Perioral numbness, tinnitus, metallic taste → seizures → arrhythmia/cardiac arrest after regional block → LAST → 20% lipid emulsion
algorithm:
Malignant hyperthermia
  → Stop volatile & sux; call for help; hyperventilate with 100% O₂ at high fresh-gas flow (change to TIVA)
  → Dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV, repeat until signs settle (up to ~10 mg/kg)
  → Active cooling; treat hyperkalaemia (insulin–dextrose, calcium), acidosis, arrhythmias (avoid CCBs); maintain urine output (myoglobinuria)
  → Later: caffeine–halothane contracture test / RYR1 genetics; counsel family
Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST)
  → Stop injection, airway + 100% O₂, benzodiazepine for seizures
  → 20% lipid emulsion: bolus 1.5 mL/kg (≈100 mL if >70 kg) over 2–3 min → infusion 0.25 mL/kg/min; repeat bolus / double infusion if unstable
  → CPR with small adrenaline doses (≤1 µg/kg); AVOID vasopressin, CCBs, β-blockers, further LA
DAS difficult intubation (2015)
  → Plan A: face-mask/intubation (≤3 + 1 attempts, videolaryngoscope)
  → Plan B: 2nd-generation supraglottic airway (≤3 attempts)
  → Plan C: final face-mask ventilation → wake patient
  → Plan D: CICO → scalpel–bougie–tube cricothyroidotomy

points: **Succinylcholine hyperkalaemia** (normal rise ~0.5 mEq/L) becomes life-threatening with receptor up-regulation: burns and major trauma/crush (after ~24–48 h), denervation (spinal cord injury, stroke, GBS), prolonged immobilisation, severe sepsis, muscular dystrophies (Duchenne → rhabdomyolysis, cardiac arrest in undiagnosed boys).

**Sugammadex**: modified γ-cyclodextrin that encapsulates rocuronium (> vecuronium); no effect on sux or benzylisoquinoliniums; 2 mg/kg (moderate), 4 mg/kg (deep), 16 mg/kg (immediate after RSI dose); reduces efficacy of hormonal contraceptives.

**Malignant hyperthermia**: AD, RYR1 (also CACNA1S); EARLIEST sign = unexplained ↑ EtCO₂ (with tachycardia); hyperthermia is late; masseter spasm; dantrolene blocks Ca²⁺ release from RyR1. Associated with central core disease, King–Denborough syndrome.

**Mallampati** (seated, mouth open, tongue protruded, no phonation): I – soft palate, fauces, uvula, pillars; II – soft palate, fauces, uvula; III – soft palate + base of uvula; IV – hard palate only. Cormack–Lehane grades the laryngoscopic view (1–4).
**LEMON**: Look externally, Evaluate 3-3-2 (mouth opening 3 fingers, hyomental 3, thyromental 2), Mallampati, Obstruction/obesity, Neck mobility. Thyromental distance <6 cm predicts difficulty.
Systemic absorption of LA (highest → lowest): intravenous > tracheal > intercostal > caudal > epidural > brachial plexus > sciatic/femoral > subcutaneous.

**Spinal vs epidural**: spinal – subarachnoid, below L1–L2 (adult cord end; L3 in neonates), small dose, fast dense block, more hypotension, PDPH (postural fronto-occipital headache; ↓ with small-gauge pencil-point needles; epidural blood patch); epidural – loss-of-resistance, catheter for continuous/segmental block (labour), ~10× dose, slower onset, test dose (lignocaine + adrenaline) detects intravascular/intrathecal placement. Tuffier's line (iliac crests) ≈ L4/L4–5.
Order of nerve block: sympathetic (B fibres) → temperature → pain → touch → motor; sympathetic level ~2 segments higher than sensory, motor ~2 lower.
**ASA fasting**: clear fluids 2 h, breast milk 4 h, infant formula / non-human milk / light meal 6 h, fried-fatty food or meat 8 h.

traps.stem: Burns patient on day 10 for dressing under GA – muscle relaxant for intubation?
traps.trap: Succinylcholine for quick intubation.
traps.fix: After ~24–48 h of burns, extra-junctional receptors → massive hyperkalaemia/arrest; use rocuronium (sugammadex for reversal).

traps.stem: Earliest sign of malignant hyperthermia under GA?
traps.trap: High temperature (name of the disease).
traps.fix: Unexplained rise in end-tidal CO₂ (with tachycardia, masseter rigidity); fever is a late sign.

traps.stem: Prolonged apnoea for 3 hours after a single dose of succinylcholine.
traps.trap: Give neostigmine to reverse.
traps.fix: Atypical pseudocholinesterase (low dibucaine number) – ventilate and sedate until it wears off; FFP supplies enzyme; neostigmine can worsen/phase II.

cards.front: Antidote for local anaesthetic systemic toxicity?
cards.back: 20% lipid emulsion – 1.5 mL/kg bolus over 2–3 min, then 0.25 mL/kg/min infusion.

cards.front: Muscle relaxant of choice in hepatic + renal failure?
cards.back: Atracurium/cisatracurium – Hofmann elimination (organ-independent).

cards.text: Sugammadex is a modified {{c1::γ-cyclodextrin}} that encapsulates {{c2::rocuronium}} (and vecuronium).

cards.front: ASA fasting time for breast milk vs formula?
cards.back: Breast milk 4 h; infant formula 6 h (clear fluids 2 h; fatty meal 8 h).

cards.front: LA causing methaemoglobinaemia?
cards.back: Prilocaine (also benzocaine).

title: Classic radiological signs & modality of choice
subject: Radiology
anchor: Sign → disease pairs are asked as image-based or match-the-following: learn the sign, the modality it appears on, and the one disease it points to
Neonate with bilious vomiting + Down syndrome + two gas bubbles, no distal gas → duodenal atresia (double bubble)
Supine ICU film with deep lucent costophrenic angle → pneumothorax (deep sulcus sign)
algorithm:
Modality of choice (common scenarios)
  → Suspected stroke: NCCT first (exclude haemorrhage); DWI-MRI most sensitive for acute infarct
  → Suspected SAH: NCCT (highly sensitive within 6 h) → LP if negative and suspicion high
  → Head injury: NCCT | Spinal cord compression / early osteomyelitis: MRI
  → PE: CT pulmonary angiography (V/Q scan if contrast contraindicated); aortic dissection: CT angiography (TEE if unstable)
  → Gallstones/acute cholecystitis: USG (HIDA scan most accurate for cholecystitis); CBD stones: MRCP
  → Renal colic: NCCT KUB | Pneumoperitoneum: erect CXR (CT most sensitive)
  → Intussusception, pyloric stenosis, DDH <6 months: USG
  → Bone metastases: Tc-99m MDP bone scan (EXCEPT myeloma – cold; use skeletal survey/whole-body MRI/PET-CT)
  → Meckel's diverticulum: Tc-99m pertechnetate scan | VUR: micturating cystourethrogram | renal scar: DMSA | split function/obstruction: DTPA/MAG3

traps.stem: Suspected skeletal metastases in multiple myeloma – best test?
traps.trap: Tc-99m MDP bone scan (standard for metastases).
traps.fix: Myeloma lesions are purely lytic with no osteoblastic response → bone scan is often negative; use skeletal survey / whole-body low-dose CT / MRI / PET-CT.

subject: Radiology
anchor: Gray = absorbed dose (J/kg); Sievert = equivalent/effective dose (biological effect) – Gy × weighting factor
Occupational limit 20 mSv/yr averaged over 5 yr (≤50 mSv in any one year); public 1 mSv/yr; lens 20 mSv/yr (ICRP 2011)
Water bright on T2, dark on T1; fat bright on both; DWI bright + ADC dark = true restricted diffusion (acute infarct)

points: **Law of Bergonié–Tribondeau**: radiosensitivity ∝ mitotic activity and inversely ∝ differentiation. Most sensitive: lymphocytes (most radiosensitive blood cell), spermatogonia, erythroblasts, bone marrow, intestinal crypts, lens (posterior subcapsular cataract); least: nerve, muscle, mature bone. Cell cycle: G2/M most sensitive, late S most resistant.
Radiosensitive tumours: seminoma, dysgerminoma, lymphoma, Ewing sarcoma, Wilms; radioresistant: osteosarcoma, melanoma.
**ALARA** – time (minimise), distance (inverse square law: doubling distance → ¼ dose), shielding (lead apron 0.25–0.5 mm Pb equivalent).

Other ICRP limits: skin/hands/feet 500 mSv/yr (occupational); declared pregnant worker – 1 mSv to the fetus for the rest of pregnancy. India (AERB) follows 20 mSv/yr averaged over 5 years with ≤30 mSv in any single year.

**Pregnancy imaging**: prefer USG and MRI (avoid gadolinium); fetal dose <50 mGy – no measurable increase in anomalies; deterministic effects (microcephaly, intellectual disability) mainly above ~100 mGy at 8–15 weeks; first 2 weeks 'all-or-none'. Necessary imaging should not be withheld; iodinated contrast allowed (check neonatal thyroid).
**Iodinated contrast reactions**: risk ↑ with prior reaction, asthma, atopy; anaphylaxis → IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (1:1000); premedication with steroid + antihistamine for prior reactors.

**Contrast-associated AKI**: creatinine rise within 48–72 h; highest risk eGFR <30; prevention = IV isotonic saline hydration (NAC/bicarbonate add no benefit); withhold metformin after contrast if eGFR <30 or AKI.
**Gadolinium**: nephrogenic systemic fibrosis in eGFR <30 (lowest risk with macrocyclic agents); brain deposition (dentate nucleus, globus pallidus) with linear agents.

**MRI contraindications**: non-MR-conditional pacemaker/ICD, ferromagnetic aneurysm clips, cochlear implants (most), metallic intra-ocular foreign body (screen welders with orbital X-ray), some neurostimulators; relative – first trimester, claustrophobia. Most prosthetic heart valves and orthopaedic implants are MR-safe/conditional.
Typical effective doses: CXR PA ~0.02 mSv; CT head ~2 mSv; CT abdomen-pelvis ~8–10 mSv; natural background ~2.4 mSv/yr (world average).
